gene:RIT1.summary: Plays a crucial role in coupling nerve growth factor (NGF) stimulation to the activation of both EPHB2 and MAPK14 signaling pathways and in NGF-dependent neuronal differentiation (PubMed:15632082). Involved in ELK1 transactivation through the Ras-MAPK signaling cascade that mediates a wide variety of cellular functions, including cell proliferation, survival, and differentiation (PubMed:23791108). Recognized by LZTR1, which mediates its ubiquitination by a BCR (BTB-CUL3-RBX1) E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex (PubMed:40934300)

disease:STX1B|driven_by|mech:loss-of-fun.explanation: Published work links STX1B-related disorders to loss of function: a deletion causing STX1B haploinsufficiency was found with myoclonic astatic epilepsy, loss-of-function variants were found in patients across the clinical range, and G226R weakens the Munc18-1 interaction and reduces release. Whether loss-of-function variants are milder is disputed: one cohort found them more often in benign syndromes, a later series found no clear genotype-phenotype correlation. Limits, attached as counter-evidence: V216E, equally severe clinically, increases fusogenicity and release probability (gain of function), and in patient-derived neurons G226R showed both gain- and loss-of-function features.

review.note: Independent AI review (Claude), not a human expert. PMID:33677401 was filed as counter-evidence, but its abstract reports three loss-of-function variants in affected individuals; it supports loss of function and only limits the genotype-phenotype split, so the AI re-reading was right and the source moved to supporting evidence (explanation reworded). PMID:42673765 (G226R shows both gain- and loss-of-function characteristics; the InDel's predicted loss of function was not detectable at single-cell level) is correctly filed as limiting; here the curators were right and the AI re-reading was not. Abstracts checked: 30737342, 26818399, 32572454, 33677401, 42673765.

Independent AI review (Claude), not a human expert. Supporting abstracts (27597756, 30266908, 33332765) do report co-aggregation of wild-type Munc18-1 by disease mutants. PMID:29538625 (no effect when overexpressed on a heterozygous background) is a genuine limit. The AI re-reading disagreed with filing the review PMID:32643187 as limiting; its sentence is neutral ('both haploinsufficiency and dominant-negative mechanisms have been proposed', mechanism 'yet to be fully understood'), so filing it as a limit on a contested dominant-negative claim is defensible. Confidence 0.5 is appropriately cautious given the direct counter-experiment.

Independent AI review (Claude), not a human expert. Abstracts 18469812, 26280581, 29538625 support haploinsufficiency. The AI re-reading disagreed with filing PMID:38242640 as limiting; the abstract calls haploinsufficiency 'the prevailing disease mechanism' but questions whether it 'alone can account for' patient heterogeneity and shows a missense mutant aggravating Doc2A/B loss, so it is correctly a limiting source. Curators right.

disease:STXBP1|driven_by|mech:protein-de.explanation: Published work links STXBP1-related disorders to protein destabilization / misfolding. Seven disease variants all had severely reduced protein levels, and at least five missense variants destabilize and aggregate Munc18-1 (C180Y is degraded by the proteasome). Limit, attached as counter-evidence: the recessive (homozygous) variant L446F affects protein stability less than heterozygous disease variants and increases synaptic transmission instead, so destabilization does not explain every variant.

review.note: Independent AI review (Claude), not a human expert. Only the explanation changed: it called the limit 'against the uniform loss-of-function model', which is about another edge; it now states the protein-stability point. Abstracts checked: 29538625, 30266908, 25284778, 18469812, 27597756, 38242640, 31855252. Note: 38242640 is about aggregation of Doc2A/B, not of Munc18-1 itself, so it is weak support.

It restored GAT-1 surface expression and GABA uptake in cell and knock-in mouse models; an early-phase trial (NCT04937062) enrols children with SLC6A1 or STXBP1 variants; and two children with deletions that include SLC6A1 had fewer epileptiform discharges after treatment (uncontrolled; cognitive impairment persisted). disease:STXBP1|shares_mechanism|disease:.explanation: Different genes, different pathways, same cell-biological problem: a subset of STXBP1 (Munc18-1) and SLC6A1 (GAT-1) missense variants make a protein that is unstable or misfolded, so it is degraded or stuck in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than working. Both have been rescued by the chemical chaperone 4-phenylbutyrate in laboratory models, and one early-phase trial (NCT04937062) enrols children with either gene on exactly this shared rationale. Important limits are attached as counter-evidence: roughly a third of SLC6A1 loss-of-function missense variants reach the cell surface normally and so cannot be helped by folding correction; no dominant-negative effect was found in SLC6A1; chemical chaperones need high, potentially toxic concentrations; the benefit may come from boosting the healthy copy rather than fixing the mutant; and the only human outcome data is two uncontrolled deletion patients. CLAUDE.md flag: G2P (G2P00036, definitive, citing the same 20619386 and 20694012) records 'gain of function'; the atlas says loss of function. Both abstracts support impaired receptor ubiquitylation (loss of ligase function), but 20694012 shows the mutant actively induces ERK/AKT signalling when wild-type CBL is reduced, a gain-of-function or dominant behaviour. As a disclosure, that sentence was added as counter-evidence and confidence lowered 0.8 -> 0.6. A human should choose the class (LoF of ligase vs GoF of signalling, or a dominant-negative/neomorphic edge).
